definition:
The Holy Spirit is God himself, present and at work in his world and among his people. The church confesses him as the third person of the Trinity, one God with the Father and the Son, not a force God uses or a mood believers feel. The creed of the Council of Constantinople (381), which most churches recite as the Nicene Creed, names him the Lord and the giver of life, who proceeds from the Father, who is worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son, and who spoke through the prophets. Scripture shows him at the beginning, when the world was still dark and empty, and at the end, calling the thirsty to come and drink. In between he gives life, equips people for God's work, speaks through the prophets, rests on the Messiah, raises Jesus from the dead, is poured out on the church at Pentecost, joins believers to Christ, makes them new, gives gifts for the good of others, and slowly shapes them into Christ's likeness.

The Hebrew word is ruach, which occurs nearly four hundred times in the Old Testament and can mean ‘wind’, ‘breath’, or ‘spirit’; context decides which. It is the wind God sends over the flood waters (Genesis 8:1), and Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones plays on all three senses at once (Ezekiel 37:1-14). The Greek pneuma has the same range, which is why Jesus can tell Nicodemus, “The wind blows where it wishes” (John 3:8) in a saying about the Spirit. The range of a word is not a hidden definition, though: the Spirit is not a wind, and Scripture speaks of him in personal terms. He teaches (John 14:26), can be grieved (Ephesians 4:30), intercedes (Romans 8:26), and apportions gifts “as He determines” (1 Corinthians 12:11). The full phrase ‘holy spirit’ (literally ‘spirit of holiness’) appears in the Old Testament only in Psalm 51:11 and Isaiah 63:10-11; far more often he is ‘the Spirit of God’ or ‘the Spirit of the LORD’. John's Gospel adds paraklētos, a person called alongside to help or plead a case, translated ‘Advocate’, ‘Helper’, ‘Counselor’, or ‘Comforter’. Jesus calls the Spirit “another Advocate” (John 14:16), and 1 John 2:1 uses the same word for Jesus himself, so the Spirit continues the presence and help that Jesus gave in person.
ot:
The Spirit appears in the Bible's second verse: “the Spirit of God was hovering over the surface of the waters” (Genesis 1:2). The verb ‘hover’ (rachaph) is used elsewhere of an eagle that “hovers over its young” (Deuteronomy 32:11). Some translations read ruach ’elohim here as ‘a wind from God’ or ‘a mighty wind’, and the Hebrew allows it; most Jewish and Christian readers have heard in it God's own life brooding over a world he is about to fill. Genesis 2:7 uses a different word for the breath God breathes into the first man (neshamah), but Job pairs the two: “The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life” (Job 33:4). The psalmist says every creature lives because God gives it breath: “When You send Your Spirit, they are created, and You renew the face of the earth” (Psalm 104:30). And the Spirit is God's presence from which no one can escape: “Where can I go to escape Your Spirit?” (Psalm 139:7).

In Israel's history the Spirit comes on particular people for particular work. Pharaoh sees in Joseph a man “in whom the Spirit of God abides” (Genesis 41:38). Bezalel, the craftsman of the tabernacle, is the first person Scripture says God “filled” with the Spirit, and the gift is skill in gold, stone, and wood (Exodus 31:3), a reminder that artistry and craft are gifts of God too. In the wilderness God takes of the Spirit that rests on Moses and places it on seventy elders, who prophesy; when Joshua wants two of them stopped, Moses answers, “I wish that all the LORD's people were prophets and that the LORD would place His Spirit on them” (Numbers 11:29). In Judges the Spirit of the LORD comes on Othniel, Gideon, Jephthah, and Samson to deliver Israel (Judges 3:10; 6:34; 11:29; 14:6). Of Gideon the Hebrew says, vividly, that the Spirit ‘clothed himself with’ Gideon. The same Spirit rushes on Saul and on David when they are anointed king (1 Samuel 10:6; 16:13), and his departure from Saul (1 Samuel 16:14) explains why David, after his sin with Bathsheba, pleads, “take not Your Holy Spirit from me” (Psalm 51:11). The Spirit also speaks. David says, “The Spirit of the LORD spoke through me” (2 Samuel 23:2), Micah is “filled with power by the Spirit of the LORD” to name Israel's sin (Micah 3:8), and the Levites' prayer in Nehemiah remembers that God's Spirit “admonished them through Your prophets” (Nehemiah 9:30). Israel also remembered the Spirit as God's presence with the whole people in the exodus, the one they “grieved” by their rebellion (Isaiah 63:10-11), and Haggai assures the returned exiles, “My Spirit remains among you” (Haggai 2:5).

The prophets look ahead to two things. First, the Spirit will rest on a coming king and servant. The shoot from Jesse's stump will carry “the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and fear of the LORD” (Isaiah 11:2); God says of his servant, “I will put My Spirit on Him” (Isaiah 42:1); and a voice says, “The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me, because the LORD has anointed Me” (Isaiah 61:1). Second, the Spirit will no longer be given to a few for a season but poured out on the whole people. Isaiah pictures the desert becoming an orchard “until the Spirit is poured out upon us from on high” (Isaiah 32:15) and hears God say, “I will pour out My Spirit on your descendants” (Isaiah 44:3). Ezekiel joins the gift to the new covenant: “I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you,” and “I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes” (Ezekiel 36:26-27). In the valley of dry bones the breath comes from the four winds and a dead nation stands up alive (Ezekiel 37:9-14). Joel widens the promise past every line Israel drew: “I will pour out My Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy” (Joel 2:28, which is 3:1 in Hebrew Bibles), servants included. Moses' wish in Numbers 11 has become God's promise.
nt:
The Gospels open with the Spirit active again. The angel tells Mary, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you” (Luke 1:35), and John the Baptist announces one who “will baptize you with the Holy Spirit” (Mark 1:8). At Jesus' baptism the Spirit descends on him like a dove (Luke 3:22), and John the Baptist says the Spirit came to rest on him (John 1:32-33), the very word Isaiah had used of the promised king. In the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus reads Isaiah 61, “The Spirit of the Lord is on Me” (Luke 4:18), and declares it fulfilled. His ministry is Spirit-driven: “if I drive out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Matthew 12:28). That is why his sternest warning concerns blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (Mark 3:28-30), which Mark ties to calling the Spirit's work in Jesus the work of an unclean spirit. Hebrews says Christ offered himself to God “through the eternal Spirit” (Hebrews 9:14), and Paul speaks of “the Spirit of Him who raised Jesus from the dead” (Romans 8:11). The Messiah is the man of the Spirit before he is the giver of the Spirit.

John's Gospel gathers Jesus' teaching on the Spirit. No one enters God's kingdom without being “born of water and the Spirit” (John 3:5). Jesus promises streams of living water, and John explains, “He was speaking about the Spirit,” who “had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:39). In the farewell discourse (John 14 to 16) Jesus promises “another Advocate” (14:16) who will be with the disciples forever, teach them and remind them of what he said (14:26), testify about him (15:26), convict the world “in regard to sin and righteousness and judgment” (16:8), and guide them into all truth (16:13). The Spirit's work points away from himself: “He will glorify Me” (16:14). On Easter evening the risen Jesus “breathed on them and said, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’” (John 20:22); the Greek verb is the one the Greek Old Testament uses in Genesis 2:7, when God breathed life into Adam.

In Acts the promise arrives. Jesus tells the disciples, “you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be My witnesses” (Acts 1:8). At Pentecost, the Feast of Weeks fifty days after Passover (Leviticus 23:15-16), a sound like wind fills the house, tongues like fire rest on each of them, and they speak in other languages that pilgrims from across the Jewish world understand (Acts 2:1-11). Peter explains it with Joel: “In the last days, God says, I will pour out My Spirit on all people” (Acts 2:17). The exalted Jesus has received the Spirit from the Father and “has poured out what you now see and hear” (Acts 2:33), and the promise belongs “to all whom the Lord our God will call to Himself” (Acts 2:39). The outpouring then crosses each boundary in turn: to Samaritans through Peter and John (Acts 8:14-17), to the Gentile household of Cornelius while Peter is still preaching (Acts 10:44-47), and to disciples of John the Baptist at Ephesus (Acts 19:6). The Spirit also directs the mission (Acts 13:2; 16:6-7) and guides the church's decisions (Acts 15:28). When Ananias lies to the Holy Spirit, Peter says, “You have not lied to men, but to God” (Acts 5:3-4).

Paul describes the Christian life as life in the Spirit. To belong to Christ is to have his Spirit: “if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Christ” (Romans 8:9). “In one Spirit we were all baptized into one body” (1 Corinthians 12:13), and only by the Spirit can anyone say “Jesus is Lord” (1 Corinthians 12:3). The Spirit makes believers God's children, crying “Abba, Father” (Galatians 4:6; Romans 8:15-16), helps them pray when they have no words (Romans 8:26), and dwells in them so that the church and each believer's body are his temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; 6:19). Believers are “sealed with the promised Holy Spirit,” who is “the pledge of our inheritance” (Ephesians 1:13-14). The word is arrabōn, a down payment that guarantees the rest, and Paul also calls the Spirit “the firstfruits” (Romans 8:23) of a harvest still to come, the resurrection of the body. The Spirit renews (Titus 3:5), produces fruit, “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22-23), and is at war with the flesh (Galatians 5:16-17). Believers “are being transformed into His image with intensifying glory, which comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18). Paul's ministry is of a new covenant, “not of the letter but of the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:6), and he gives the church the triadic blessing that names the Spirit with the Son and the Father (2 Corinthians 13:14; compare Matthew 28:19). The Spirit also gives gifts for the body's good (1 Corinthians 12 to 14), which the study on the gifts of the Spirit takes up. Peter says the prophets “spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1:21). Revelation ends each of its letters to the churches with the charge to hear “what the Spirit says to the churches” (Revelation 2:7), and in its last chapter “The Spirit and the bride say, ‘Come!’” (Revelation 22:17).

keyTexts.why: The Spirit of God hovers over the unformed world. The Bible's first mention of the Spirit places him at creation as the presence of God's life and power.
God shares the Spirit on Moses with seventy elders, and Moses wishes that all the LORD's people had the Spirit. The wish becomes a promise in Joel and is fulfilled at Pentecost.
The Spirit rushes on David at his anointing and departs from Saul. In the Old Testament the Spirit equips leaders for their office and can be withdrawn.
One of only two Old Testament passages to use the phrase ‘holy spirit’. David joins the plea for a clean heart to the plea not to lose God's Spirit.
The Spirit will rest on the coming son of David and give him wisdom, counsel, strength, and the fear of the LORD. The Gospels see this fulfilled at Jesus' baptism.
God promises a new heart and his own Spirit within his people, so that they walk in his ways. It is the Old Testament's clearest link between the Spirit and inward renewal.
God will pour out his Spirit on all people, sons and daughters, old and young, servants included. Peter quotes it to explain Pentecost.
Jesus reads Isaiah 61 in the synagogue at Nazareth and says it is fulfilled in him. He is the one anointed with the Spirit whom the prophets promised.

Jesus promises another Advocate, the Spirit of truth, who will be with his disciples forever, teach them, and remind them of his words. The foundation of the church's teaching that the Spirit is personal.
The Spirit convicts the world, guides the apostles into truth, and glorifies Christ. His work always points to the Son.
The Spirit is poured out at Pentecost, the disciples speak in other languages, and Peter proclaims that the exalted Jesus has sent the Spirit promised by Joel to all whom God calls.
Paul's fullest account of life in the Spirit: freedom from condemnation, the indwelling Spirit, adoption, the Spirit as firstfruits of the resurrection, and his intercession in weakness.
Only by the Spirit can anyone confess Jesus as Lord. One Spirit gives many gifts and baptizes believers into one body.
The Spirit against the flesh, and the fruit of the Spirit. Growth in Christlike character is the Spirit's work in those who walk by him.
Believers are sealed with the Spirit, the pledge of their inheritance. The Spirit is God's guarantee that he will finish what he has begun.

history:
The earliest Christians baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19) and prayed and praised in that threefold pattern before they had settled vocabulary for it. The Nicene Creed of 325 ended simply with belief in the Holy Spirit, because the debate at Nicaea was over the Son. In the following decades some who accepted the Son's full deity denied the Spirit's, treating him as a creature or a ministering power; opponents called them Pneumatomachians, ‘Spirit-fighters’, and they are often linked with Macedonius of Constantinople. Athanasius answered them in his Letters to Serapion (about 359 to 361), arguing that the one who makes creatures holy and gives them life cannot himself be a creature. Basil of Caesarea's On the Holy Spirit (about 375) defended giving glory to the Spirit together with the Father and the Son, and Gregory of Nazianzus's fifth Theological Oration (Oration 31, 380) confessed the Spirit plainly as God. The Council of Constantinople in 381 expanded the creed's third article to confess the Spirit as Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father, worshiped and glorified with the Father and the Son. The council described the Spirit's rank by his worship and his works rather than by the word homoousios, but the church has always read the article as confessing his full deity.

The creed became the occasion of the church's longest division over the Spirit. Western theology, following Augustine's On the Trinity, taught that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, the bond of love between them, while Augustine also held that he proceeds principally from the Father. The Third Council of Toledo in Spain (589) recited the creed with the Latin word filioque, ‘and the Son’. The phrase spread through the Frankish church, and in 1014 it entered the creed as sung in Rome. Eastern theologians, most sharply Photius of Constantinople in the ninth century, objected both to the theology, which they held confused the Father's unique role as source, and to the West altering an ecumenical creed on its own authority. The filioque was among the causes of the division between East and West usually dated to 1054. The Council of Florence (1439) reached a union that the Eastern churches did not receive, and the question remains open between Orthodox and Western churches today.

Medieval theology reflected at length on the Spirit's gifts and on grace, and Thomas Aquinas treated the seven gifts drawn from the Greek and Latin text of Isaiah 11:2-3 as the Spirit's work making believers ready to follow his promptings. The Reformers gave the Spirit's work in salvation new prominence. John Calvin opened the third book of his Institutes (final edition 1559) by teaching that the Spirit is the bond by which Christ unites believers to himself, and he taught that the Spirit's inner testimony persuades believers that Scripture is God's word (Institutes 1.7). Martin Luther, facing radicals such as the Zwickau prophets (1521 to 1522) who claimed direct revelations, insisted that God gives his Spirit through the outward Word and sacraments, not apart from them; his Against the Heavenly Prophets (1525) argued the point. The Puritan John Owen wrote the most extensive English treatment of the Spirit's person and work, his Pneumatologia (1674). John Wesley's teaching on the witness of the Spirit and assurance, and Jonathan Edwards's analysis of genuine and counterfeit religious experience in Religious Affections (1746), shaped the evangelical revivals.

Modern Pentecostalism traces its beginnings to Charles Parham's Bible school in Topeka, Kansas (1901), and above all to the Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles (1906) led by William J. Seymour, a Black holiness preacher. The charismatic renewal carried similar experiences into historic denominations from the 1960s, including the Roman Catholic Church from 1967, and Pentecostal and charismatic Christians now number in the hundreds of millions worldwide, especially in Africa, Latin America, and Asia. The Second Vatican Council's Lumen Gentium (1964) taught that the Spirit distributes gifts among the faithful of every rank. Meanwhile theologians in many traditions returned to the Spirit's place in the Trinity, in creation, and in the church's hope. The questions that divide these traditions are taken up below and on the site's page on the Holy Spirit and his gifts.

differ.view: The Western confession: from the Father and the Son
differ.body: Roman Catholic, Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, and most other Western churches confess that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. They point out that the New Testament calls him both the Spirit of God and “the Spirit of Christ” (Romans 8:9), that the Son sends him from the Father (John 15:26; 16:7), and that the risen Jesus breathes him on the disciples (John 20:22). If the Son's sending in history reflects who the Spirit eternally is, the Spirit's relation to the Son is eternal too. Following Augustine, they see the Spirit as the love shared between Father and Son, which safeguards that the Son is equal with the Father in all things but being the Father. Many Western theologians today acknowledge that the unilateral insertion of the phrase into the creed was irregular, and some Western churches recite the creed without it in ecumenical settings.

differ.view: The Eastern confession: from the Father
differ.body: The Orthodox churches confess, in the words of the creed of 381 as it was agreed, that the Spirit proceeds from the Father. Jesus himself says the Spirit “proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26). The Father is the one source within the Godhead: the Son is begotten of him and the Spirit proceeds from him, and to add the Son as a source of the Spirit's being blurs the distinction of persons and tends to make the Spirit subordinate, a mere link between the other two. The Son does send the Spirit into the world and the Spirit rests on the Son, and many Orthodox theologians accept that the Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son in the sense of his manifestation and mission. What they reject is the claim that the Son shares in being the eternal source of the Spirit, and the West's changing of a common creed without a common council.

differ.view: Spirit baptism as a distinct empowering after conversion
differ.body: Classical Pentecostals, with roots in the Wesleyan holiness movement's teaching on a second work of grace, hold that baptism in the Spirit is an experience of empowering for witness that follows conversion, promised to every believer and to be sought. They read Acts as a pattern: the disciples believed in Jesus before Pentecost, the Samaritans believed and were baptized before the Spirit fell on them (Acts 8:14-17), and the Ephesian disciples received the Spirit when Paul laid hands on them (Acts 19:1-7). Jesus' promise concerns power to be witnesses (Acts 1:8). The Assemblies of God (founded 1914) and many other Pentecostal bodies confess speaking in tongues as the initial physical evidence of this baptism, while many charismatics hold the second experience without that requirement.

differ.view: Spirit baptism as part of becoming a Christian
differ.body: Most Reformed, Baptist, and other evangelical Christians, along with many charismatics, hold that every believer is baptized in the Spirit at conversion. Paul says, “in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body” (1 Corinthians 12:13), and “if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Christ” (Romans 8:9). Pentecost was the once-for-all turn of the ages, and the delayed gifts in Samaria and Ephesus mark the gospel crossing new boundaries under apostolic witness rather than a pattern for every believer. James D. G. Dunn's Baptism in the Holy Spirit (1970) argued this at length. Fresh fillings for boldness and service (Acts 4:31; Ephesians 5:18) are repeated and expected, but they are not a second initiation.

differ.view: The Spirit given through the rites of initiation
differ.body: Roman Catholic, Orthodox, and some Anglican and Lutheran Christians connect the gift of the Spirit closely with baptism and with the laying on of hands or anointing that accompanies or follows it, called confirmation in the West and chrismation in the East. They point to Acts 2:38, where repentance and baptism are joined to “the gift of the Holy Spirit”, to the laying on of hands in Acts 8 and 19, and to Paul's language of anointing and sealing (2 Corinthians 1:21-22). The Spirit is given to the whole church and to each member through the means Christ appointed, and confirmation or chrismation strengthens the baptized for witness. In this view the renewed longing for the Spirit's power that Pentecostals express is welcome, and it finds its home in the church's sacramental life.

errors:
The church has rejected every teaching that makes the Spirit less than God. The fourth-century Pneumatomachians, who counted him a creature or a created power, were answered by Athanasius, Basil, and the Council of Constantinople in 381, because only God can give divine life, make holy, and be worshiped. The same judgment falls on modern teachings that call the holy spirit an impersonal force or energy (the view of Jehovah's Witnesses, for example), since Scripture speaks of the Spirit teaching, grieving, interceding, and choosing, and Peter treats lying to the Spirit as lying to God (Acts 5:3-4). Modalism, the idea that Father, Son, and Spirit are only three roles or masks of one person, was rejected because the Son prays to the Father and sends the Spirit, and the three are distinct though never divided.

The church has also resisted claims that set the Spirit against the Word he inspired. Montanism in the later second century announced a new age of the Spirit through its prophets whose words were treated as surpassing the apostles, and the church judged it a false prophecy. Luther made the same judgment against the radicals of his day who claimed revelations apart from Scripture. The Spirit's own test is that he glorifies Christ and confesses that Jesus came in the flesh (John 16:14; 1 John 4:1-2), so any spirit that leads away from the Christ of Scripture is not the Holy Spirit. Two opposite mistakes are also common. One reduces the Spirit to spectacle, as if his presence were measured only by the dramatic. The other reduces him to a doctrine to be affirmed while the church runs on its own strength. Scripture gives both the Spirit who shakes the house at Pentecost and the Spirit who makes people patient, gentle, and faithful. Some anxious believers fear they have committed the unforgivable sin; Jesus' warning in Mark 3:28-30 concerns hardened hostility that calls the Spirit's work in Jesus evil, and pastors have long counseled that a troubled fear of having done so is itself a sign of a heart the Spirit has not abandoned.
life:
The doctrine of the Spirit means that God is not distant from the Christian life. The same Spirit who hovered over the waters and raised Jesus from the dead lives in every believer, so the Christian is never simply left to try harder. Prayer is possible even when words run out, because the Spirit intercedes (Romans 8:26), and the cry ‘Abba, Father’ is his work in the heart, not a feeling a person has to manufacture. Scripture can be read with expectation, because the Spirit who carried the prophets along still opens it to readers. Growth is slow and real, like fruit, and it looks like love, patience, and self-control more than like excitement.

It also means that no one in the church is a spectator. The Spirit was poured out on sons and daughters, old and young, servants and free, and he gives each believer some part in building up the others. And it gives hope. The Spirit is the down payment and the firstfruits; what he does now is a foretaste of the resurrection of the body and the renewal of all things. A believer who grieves, doubts, or feels spiritually dry is still sealed by the Spirit for the day of redemption (Ephesians 4:30), and the Spirit's presence does not depend on the strength of a person's feelings.
questions: In the Old Testament the Spirit comes on particular people for particular tasks, and the prophets promise he will be poured out on all God's people. What changes at Pentecost, and what stays the same?
Jesus says the Spirit “will glorify Me” (John 16:14). How might that help a church tell the difference between the Spirit's work and mere excitement or mere routine?
Paul lists the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22-23. Which of these do you most need, and what does it mean that they are called fruit rather than achievements?
